Security services sold to enterprises and through partners

LevelBlue sells cybersecurity services and technology: managed detection and response, network security, consulting and its USM platform. It sells to enterprise buyers directly and through managed security service provider partners.
The two groups read different parts of the website. Product pages tell an enterprise seller what an account cares about, while partner-program research matters more to a channel account manager.
Only a small share of visitors ever filled out a form. Marketing was bringing in the right organizations, but sellers had no view of who they were or what they were reading.

Preparing for an account also meant checking several places. Sales-enablement material sat in Binder, and account history and other context lived elsewhere. The team needed that information within easy reach and a way to know when a target account was showing interest.

Among the accounts that surfaced were a large equipment-rental company with visits from several locations and a managed security partner reading up on the channel program. Persona definitions and ZoomInfo lookup helped find the right contacts.

At the same time, LevelBlue set up a Microsoft Teams assistant trained on Binder material and its public website. Sellers could ask it which accounts had visited, or ask product questions, without leaving the tool they already used.
Jenny Galinski · Marketing, LevelBlue
Putting it into practice

The channel team could use partner-program activity to prepare for a conversation with an MSSP. Direct sellers could see which topics an enterprise account was researching and pull up the sales material to match.

A seller can start by asking whether a named account has visited recently and what it looked at. The assistant pulls that together with product and pricing information, so the seller does less digging.
Marketing now sees which accounts are engaging, and sales has a practical way to prepare. The planned CRM and outreach integrations would build on that.

With the personas in place, the team could write outreach that fit each buyer. Reps got personalized email sequences and could prospect on LinkedIn through the Chrome extension, working the same contacts marketing had prepared.

QX Global Group researches each target company before the first sales email goes out

QX sells into small, hand-picked groups of companies in specialized industries. MarketBetter helped turn those lists into enriched audiences and personalized email sequences, starting with 162 Senior Living contacts and later adding event and regional finance-buyer campaigns.

QX had to tell apart buyer groups that look alike on paper, such as finance leaders at multifamily housing companies and finance leaders in other residential markets. Broad intent categories and generic emails tend to blur that line.

The campaign paired a research agent with a four-touch email sequence. Before writing anything, the agent looked at each company for likely finance and accounting problems: a slow close process, complicated reporting, heavy AP/AR work, staffing pressure. The opening lines drew on what it found.

The team set up AI Context with QX’s target markets, use cases and answers to common objections. Every email draft and every fit check drew on that same brief, so different campaigns described the business the same way.
By September 2026, campaign records showed event and regional finance-buyer outreach, with 456 sent or replied email entries across 325 recipients. Those numbers count activity. They are not revenue.
